title: BBC News Anchor Maryam Moshiri Reveals Blood Cancer Diagnosis
full_text: Sep 7, 2026 7:42am PT BBC News Anchor Maryam Moshiri Reveals Blood Cancer Diagnosis By K.J. Yossman Plus Icon K.J. Yossman @KJYossman Latest ‘SNL U.K.’ Adds Freddie Meredith to Cast 4 hours ago ‘Fauda’ Creator Calls Mark Ruffalo a ‘Rare Combination’ of ‘Stupid’ and ‘Ignorant’ After His Viral Statement on Paramount: ‘Do You Understand What It Means, “Genocide”?’ 3 days ago ‘Game of Thrones’ Creator George R.R. Martin Confirms Play ‘The Mad King’ Will Transfer to London 3 days ago See All BBC BBC News anchor Maryam Moshiri has revealed she has been diagnosed with incurable blood cancer. The anchor, who joined the BBC in 2003, has covered events ranging from the Pope’s funeral to the Iran war since being diagnosed with Polycythaemia vera (PV) two years ago. Moshiri went public with her diagnosis Monday in an interview with The Times of London. “I was working 14-hour days, constantly on air, constantly having to think on my feet, and holding it together, despite the fact that I had this chronic tiredness and fatigue,” she told the newspaper. “When you’re doing live news, you have this rush of adrenaline, and you just have to get on with it.” Related Stories Telluride Festival Lineup: 'The Debut,' 'Elsinore' and 'Tender Loving Care' Set for Premieres, Tributes for John Malkovich, Sandra Hüller and Andrew Haigh Telluride’s Julie Huntsinger on Her 20 Years Leading the Festival, Chasing ‘Digger’ and ‘Dune 3’ and a ‘True TBA’ Film Hidden Until Patrons Walk Into the Theater Although the cancer itself is not deadly, PV results in the overproduction of red blood cells, causing the blood to thicken and potentially leading to blood clots, heart attacks and strokes. It requires lifelong treatment, much of which is physically gruelling. Popular on Variety “It is going to be there till the day I die,” Moshiri said of her diagnosis. “A big part of this disease is having to get on with life.” Among the treatments Moshiri has endured are twice-monthly venesections, where doctors remove blood through a vein, which she said was exhausting and left her feeling “extremely unwell.” Despite that, she travelled to Rome for two weeks last year to cover the death of Pope Francis. On her return she underwent an immunotherapy treatment which resulted in “horrendous” side effects. She eventually switched to a different drug. Moshri, who also has three children, decided to go public with her diagnosis in order to back a campaign by charity Blood Cancer U.K. called “Here for This,” which highlights the time sufferers miss with loved ones due to their treatment. She is also determined to continue working. “I love what I do. I love being where the story is,” she told The Times. “I don’t want to allow blood cancer to stop me from doing my work.” Starz’s U.K.-Set Boxing Crime Drama ‘Fightland’ Is a Knockout: TV Review Loading comments... title: Tokyo Film Festival Adds New Initiatives, Kashiko Kawakita Award to Honor Women in Cinema
full_text: × Skip to main content By Abid Rahman Plus Icon Abid Rahman International Editor, Digital gentlemanabroad Follow Sign Up View All September 7, 2026 7:39am Sahoko Hata Tokyo International Film Festival The Tokyo International Film Festival (TIFF) is adding a series of new initiatives for its 39th edition. The festival is adding two new awards for the Nippon Cinema Now section; launching a new section titled Crosscut Asia +; and establishing the Kashiko Kawakita Award to honor women in cinema. The festival says the new initiatives “aim to enhance the global reach of Japanese cinema, foster next-generation talent and co-creation across Asia, and promote the preservation and continuation of diverse film cultures.” The two new awards linked to Nippon Cinema Now include best film and a special jury prize. The festival is looking to draw more attention to local talent and “provide stronger support for undiscovered Japanese talent— from promising newcomers to visionary veterans—and to bring their work to worldwide audiences.” Related Stories Movies 'Primetime,' Chris Rock's 'Misty Green' and Latest Paul Thomas Anderson Movie Join London Film Festival Lineup TV How a Sweet, Horny Hockey Show Rewrote the Rules of Independent TV “Through the establishment of a new competition within the Nippon Cinema Now section, we will shine a spotlight on exceptional new Japanese talent and introduce them to the world,” Takeo Hisamatsu, TIFF’s festival director, said in a statement. “We hope to give creators the courage to take on their next challenge while empowering them to advance to the global stage. By serving as a platform for emerging talent to take flight, the Tokyo International Film Festival aims to contribute to the growth and development of the Japanese film industry.” Crosscut Asia+ will be a new section at TIFF for 2026 is a joint initiative with the Japan Foundation, and highlights Southeast Asian cinema. The section carries on the work of a former Tokyo section, the Japan Foundation Asia Center presents Crosscut Asia, which ran from 2014 to 2019. Crosscut Asia+ “will feature a curated selection of films jointly chosen by vibrant film programmers from both the region and Japan, centered around a unique, annual theme from their distinct perspectives.” For the inaugural edition of Crosscut Asia+, programmers Raslene (Indonesia) and Ueda Masayuki (Japan) will present six films under the theme ‘Side by Side,’ featuring a lineup that ranges from timeless classics to recent releases. Included in the lineup are Rafael Manuel’s Filipiñana , Kamila Andini’s Four Seasons in Java , Polen Ly’s Becoming Human , Bachtiar Siagian’s Turang , Daniel Hui’s Small Hours of the Night , and Hafiz Rancajale’s Behind The Flickering Light: The Archive . For 2026, TIFF is also establishing the Kashiko Kawakita Award to honor women in cinema, and the organizer’s revealed that Sahoko Hata will be the inaugural honoree. The award was established by the Kawakita Memorial Film Institute and was conceived as a recognition “by women, for women“ as an “achievement award [that] honors individuals who have been advancing film culture both in Japan and internationally.” The award pays tribute to Kawakita Kashiko — affectionately known as “Madame Kawakita”— a trailblazing woman who bridged East and West through cinema and who played a pivotal role in founding the Japan Film Library Council and the National Film Archive of Japan. Honoree Hata, is an acclaimed Japanese critic who fostered filmic links between her country and France. The now 95-year-old began her career in the 1950s and was a key figure in Japanese film culture, who helped purchase and bring landmark French New Wave films such as Breathless , Purple Noon and Mon Oncle to Japan. “When I was first approached about receiving the 1st Kashiko Kawakita Award, my initial decision was to decline,” said Hata in a statement. “Throughout the pre-war and post-war eras — a time when women were not even permitted to participate — Mme. Kawakita was active with her own distinct eye for importing, exporting, and above all, selecting films. Her legacy remains a page in film history, as well as a chapter in the history of women. On one occasion, Mme. Kawakita whispered to me: “As women, there are so many moments where we must endure, aren’t there?” They were profound words indeed. It is precisely because I felt a compelling desire to pass this story on that I resolved to accept the award.” The Tokyo Film Festival runs from Oct. 26 to Nov. 4. THR

title: ‘You Can See Everything’ Review: Elizabeth Holmes Doc From Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim Is Fascinatingly Slippery, Dizzyingly Clever
full_text: × Skip to main content By Angie Han Plus Icon Angie Han Television Critic ajhan Follow Sign Up View All September 7, 2026 7:36am 'You Can See Everything' A24 Elizabeth Holmes would like you to know that she has never lied. Not just about Theranos — about anything ever, she insists, her startlingly large eyes shining with conviction. She’s only been misunderstood because she thinks so differently, or misrepresented by outside parties pushing their own cynical agenda. You Can See Everything , a new documentary about the billionaire turned convicted fraudster, is ostensibly her attempt to change all that. In the spirit of radical transparency, she intends to finally get her real story out there, once and for all. Related Stories Movies Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim's Elizabeth Holmes Doc 'You Can See Everything': First Reactions Movies 'Carl Sagan: We Are Made of Star Stuff' Review: Nanette Burstein's NatGeo Doc Prioritizes the Human Over the Intellectual, for Better and Worse You Can See Everything The Bottom Line Smart, funny and full of surprises. Venue: Telluride Film Festival Directors: Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim 2 hours 54 minutes But if you’ve ever seen anything by its directors, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim , you’ll already know better than to expect something so simple. What begins as a fascinatingly intimate portrait of a deluded or disingenuous scammer reveals as something even wilder, more ambitious and less predictable, until we’re left to ponder what value a personal truth has at all. The nearly three-hour film, which had its world premiere at the Telluride Film Festival, splits cleanly into two halves. In the first and more straightforward, Fielder (and Oppenheim, and their crew, though of that contingent it’s only Fielder we see regularly) essentially embed in the beachside San Diego rental where Holmes, her partner Billy Evans and their two young children are enjoying the last weeks before Holmes is due to report to a Texas federal prison for an 11-year sentence. There, You Can See Everything is only too happy to satisfy the voyeuristic curiosity that probably brought you here in the first place. Fielder seems to be lurking behind every doorframe and around every corner, taking in every emotional conversation or casually intimate moment. (The couple’s very different approaches to scrambling eggs turns out to be weirdly telling.) His high tolerance for awkwardness means he’s willing to ask the questions we’re all thinking but might hesitate to pose ourselves — like “ Why ?” when Evans speaks about choosing to be a part of Holmes’ life essentially at first sight, despite the very public and sordid details of her then-recent downfall. Fielder’s presence in front of the camera (and eventually in their guest room, which comes with no mattress because Evans claims to prefer sleeping on bare bedframes) also means You Can See Everything dispenses with any pretense of “objectivity.” What it aims for, instead, is a kind of authenticity — the sense that it’s earnestly trying to understand Holmes’ mind and motives, even if the filmmakers don’t appear to believe for a second that she’s as innocent as she says; that Holmes really is trying her best to communicate her line of thinking, even if it requires Olympic-level mental gymnastics to justify it. The documentary’s time with the family is fruitful, in that they reveal Holmes’ psychology as a fleeting paparazzi photo or a carefully managed puff piece never could. And were You Can See Everything just a profile of Holmes on the eve of her sentence, it would be a captivating if slightly baggy document in itself, with no shortage of moments to make you groan or goggle your eyes. But it’s the second half, which picks up two years later, where the movie really kicks into gear. Its abrupt turns are so deliciously surprising I’m loath to give away too much detail. But I’ll say broadly that it gets excitingly meta and almost surreal in confronting the fact that Holmes is now in prison, and therefore unable to speak for herself in any length or depth. Control of her narrative has once again slipped outside her hands, and in her absence, the void gets filled by other means. One is Evans, who’s all too happy to speak on his partner’s behalf, down to posting as her from her verified X account. He doesn’t even need to consult with her to say what she thinks about this or feels about that, because their souls are just that united — never mind that he’s clearly an angry boor with controlling tendencies, or that he disregards her actual, previously-stated-on-the-record opinions whenever they’re inconvenient. Remember what I said about this film not pretending to be objective? It makes no bones about the fact that it absolutely loathes this guy. Another sticky version of Holmes’ narrative is the Hulu show The Dropout ; though it came out before Holmes’ incarceration, it continues to shape the public’s perception of her to a degree that all the other articles and books and podcasts about her have not. Just ask the barber who explains the plot of the miniseries to Billy during a cut and shave. But yet another, You Can See Everything is shrewd enough to realize, is itself. Even as Holmes has tried to explain herself, our understanding of her has already been filtered through the questions Fielder asks, through his and Oppenheim’s impression of her level of sincerity, through the choices they’ve made about which interactions to leave in and which to cut out. There’s also the barest suggestion that Fielder may have an eensy crush on Holmes — though the fact that the picture hints at said crush without stating it outright could just be another pointed example of how easily we can be manipulated into inferring the thoughts and feelings of other people. An increasing reliance on simulacra (supposedly necessitated by Holmes’ absence, but you’re not going to convince me the guy behind The Rehearsal wasn’t just dying to reenact some conversations in a recreation of the Bryan Federal Prison visitors room) adds another giddy layer of artificiality in this ostensible search for truth — as does the introduction of a third co-conspirator who lightly interrogates Fielder in the way he once did Holmes, and finds he’s as capable of evasiveness as anyone else. In one scene, this new colleague and Fielder find themselves outraged on Holmes’ behalf that a crass X response posted by Evans through her account “does not sound like her.” They’re almost certainly right, based on what we’ve seen of Holmes — and they also have about as much authority to determine what Holmes would or would not say as anyone who isn’t Holmes herself does. You Can See Everything reaches for accuracy in its portrayal of a much talked-about figure. It ends up asking, with plenty of humor but no small amount of wisdom, what “accuracy” would even look like in the first place. Full credits Venue: Telluride Film Festival Distributor: A24 Production companies: Blow Out Productions, To Be Formed Productions Directors: Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim Producers: Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, Tatiana Bears, Maggie Ambrose, Jack Davis Executive producer: Emily Osborne Director of photography: David Bolen Production designer: Alex DiGerlando Editor: Adam Locke-Norton Music: Ari Balouzian 2 hours 54 minutes THR

title: Vertical Video Studio LoveHit Launches With Adaptations Of Literary Classics Starring Microdrama Regulars & Eric Roberts
full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse ‘SNL UK’ Adds Comedian & ‘Big Boys’ Actor Freddie Meredith To Season 2 Cast Dori Media Wants Buyers To Hunt ‘New Love’ At MIPCOM Dvizhon Studios Launches With Sex Education Series ‘The First Time’ A Featuring Puppet Presenter, Ukraine War Veteran & Social Media Star Tumazar View All September 7, 2026 7:15am Ethan Vaughan and Jean Evans in 'Wuthering Heights' Aleksandar Sekulic EXCLUSIVE: Literary classics such as Wuthering Heights and Jane Eyre are getting the microdrama treatment. This is through the latest entrant into the microdrama field, LoveHit , an L.A.-based studio and app focused on originals based on classic literary adaptations. LoveHit, which launches this month, has a vertical video slate built entirely from classic novels in the public domain. At launch, this will comprise Wuthering Heights , Pride and Prejudice , Jane Eyre , The Great Gatsby and Beauty and the Beast . More are in post-production, including Dangerous Liaisons , The Scarlett Letter and Les Misérables . Related Stories News David Oyelowo & Nate Parker's Mansa Studios Debuts Slate Of TikTok Microdramas News Kevin Hart's Hartbeat To House Vertical Originals On Microdrama Platform aTwist Each has been written, shot and edited as both a vertical series and a horizontial features, with the latter being readied for TV and streaming buyers worldwide attending MIPCOM on October 12-15 in Cannes. Series will last roughly 50 episodes running between one and three minutes, with the films at 90 minutes. Watch on Deadline Actors appearing in the titles include microdrama regulars Meg Bush, Tyler Harlow and Sophie Swiszcz, along film, television and stage stars. These include Academy Award nominee Eric Roberts, who appears in Jane Eyre , which stars Raina Silver and Tyler Harlow. Ethan Vaughan and Jean Evans will star in Wuthering Heights , which is relocated to a present day American ranch. A vertical cut of the show launched on the LoveHit app on August 27 ahead of the full launch. Other plotlines see Dangerous Liaisons adapted in a story where a Manhattan socialite hires the anonymous author of a scandalous blog to destroy her ex-fiancé’s reputation. The Scarlett Letters follows a woman who believes her husband died overseas only to fall for the young pastor helping her rebuild, while Les Misérables moves the story into college, following a student who loses everything before finding anonymity and income behind a webcam, only for someone to recognize her. “There isn’t a market in the world where these titles need much of an introduction,” said Lenny Levi, CEO of LoveHit. “Every generation has adapted them, and every generation finds its own reason to connect with them. That’s what makes them evergreen.” We hear LoveHit has been privately financed, with a group of investors supportive of the company’s growth and content strategy. Levi is an L.A.-based film and media producer with more than 15 years across production, business affairs, international distribution and emerging media. He has worked at Sony Pictures Entertainment, CBS Television Studios, Paramount Television Studios and Riot Games. He has produced multiple feature films and currently focuses on film and vertical storytelling. He was closely involved in building and launching Squad.App, an AI-powered influencer marketing platform for brands and creators. He has also produced feature films. “We framed everything for both formats and cut two versions: the vertical version is made specifically for mobile devices and has its own way of telling the story, while the horizontal version goes to Cannes, where we’re already seeing interest in romance from television and streaming buyers around the world. I’m especially proud that we shot all of it in Los Angeles, using local casts and crews.” There have been a spate of L.A.-based microdrama businesses launching over recent weeks, and LoveHit’s launch comes less than a week after aTwist , which is led by a trio of former network execs, debuted. aTwist debuted on September 3 with titles such as Buried Alive, Back For Revenge , Cash Out , Hollywood Starlet , I Fell in Love with a Dragon Prince , I Swiped Right on a Serial Killer , My Billionaire Kidney , My Book Boyfriend Came to Life , Pretty Hurts and So Do I , Something is Alive in My Attic and Strangers, a Plane and a Deadly Game . It also has a production partnership with Kevin Hart’s Hartbeat, a deal with BET and the first microdrama from The Bold and the Beautiful ‘s creative chief, Bradley Bell. title: ‘Primetime,’ Chris Rock’s ‘Misty Green’ and Latest Paul Thomas Anderson Movie Join London Film Festival Lineup
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 7, 2026 7:00am Robert Pattinson as Chris Hansen in 'Primetime' BFI London Film Festival Hot off its Venice Film Festival premiere, Robert Pattinson ‘s Primetime is set to take on the BFI London Film Festival next month. The Oct. 7-18 event has unveiled even more additions to its starry, jam-packed lineup, including the U.K. premiere of Paul Thomas Anderson’s Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall , the Oscar winner’s intimate recording of the Geese frontman’s solo piano performance at the legendary New York concert hall. The previously announced Artificial , starring Andrew Garfield and directed by Luca Guadagnino, is getting a Gala premiere with talent expected to attend. The movie chronicles the consequential days leading up to the sudden firing and reinstatement of Sam Altman as CEO of OpenAI. Related Stories TV How a Sweet, Horny Hockey Show Rewrote the Rules of Independent TV Movies Laura Poitras Shares the Desperate Vision Behind Her ICE Documentary 'They're Here': "What's Happening in the United States Is a Nightmare" From director-screenwriter Chris Rock is Misty Green in the fest’s “Journey” strand, starring Rosalind Eleazar, Adam Driver and Daniel Kaluuya. The comedy follows Eleazar as the titular character, stuck in the throes of a fading career, who has an old acquaintance re-enter her life. Also set to screen in London Film Festival ‘s “Create” strand is the latest documentary from Oscar winner Jonathan Glazer, titled Joy of Joys . The project intersperses clips from Abbey Road, where London schoolchildren film recording sessions with artists including Olivia Rodrigo, Arctic Monkeys and Jarvis Cocker, with daily recordings from kids in Gaza, Sudan, Ukraine and Yemen. Another doc, Everest: The Other Side , joins LFF’s “Journey” strand, following a mountaineering couple with a shared passion and ambition for the near-impossible from directors Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin. Finally, Inherit , from Banjong Pisanthanakun about a rich Thai family who fall apart with the arrival of a distant relative, will premiere in the “Cult” strand. The horror features a magnetic performance from Davika Hoorne. The BFI London Film Festival added sit-down discussions with Javier Bardem, star of the festival circuit’s Bunker , and Robert Eggers, gearing up to release the hotly anticipated Nosferatu follow-up Werwulf , to their Screen Talks slate. Check out the full Screen Talks lineup with Andrew Scott, Cynthia Erivo, Mahershala Ali, Jesse Eisenberg and more here . The world premieres from this year’s BFI London Film Festival include Brad Bird’s Ray Gunn and Travis Knight’s Wildwood , as well as star-powered screenings of Ink , Wild Horse Nine , Club Kid , Paper Tiger , Possible Love , Bunker , Tender Loving Care and more. The festival will open with Elsinore and close with The Debut . THR

title: Paul Thomas Anderson’s Cameron Winter Concert Film Joins London Film Festival Lineup As Mubi Acquires World Rights
full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac Paul Thomas Anderson’s Cameron Winter Concert Film Joins London Film Festival Lineup As Mubi Acquires World Rights Lee Chang-Dong’s ‘Possible Love’ Earns 6.5-Minute Ovation At Venice World Premiere A24’s ‘Primetime’, Starring Robert Pattinson As Chris Hansen, Lands 9-Minute Ovation At Venice World Premiere View All September 7, 2026 7:00am 'Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall' Mubi The London Film Festival has made several additions to this year’s lineup, including the concert film Paul Thomas Anderson shot at Carnegie Hall last year with Geese frontman Cameron Winter . Mubi has now also acquired global rights outside of North America to the film. Scroll down for the full list of LFF additions. Officially titled Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall, the film was shot during Winter’s sold-out solo run at Carnegie Hall in December 2025. Images of Anderson roaming around the concert venue with a large 35mm camera were shared widely on social media sites at the time. Filmmaker Bennie Safdie was also seen lurking at the shows with a camera. The Good Time filmmaker has now been listed as a producer on the project alongside Sara Murphy, Erica Frauman and Maggie Ambrose. Related Stories News London Film Festival Lineup: Ava DuVernay's '14th' & Boots Riley's 'I Love Boosters' Among Headline Titles -- Full List Festivals Hirokazu Kore-eda, Carol Morley & Lili Horvát In Competition At London Film Festival The concert film will screen as part of LFF’s Create strand. It will be the UK premiere. The film will drop on Mubi in 2027. Janus/Criterion are releasing the film in North America. Watch on Deadline The LFF has also added a series of new screen talks. Javier Bardem and Robert Eggers will now also participate in screen talks. Bardem has two films that will screen at the LFF: The Beloved and Bunker . Eggers is set to debut his latest feature, Werwulf , on New Year’s Day. This year’s LFF will run from October 7 to 18. The festival will open with the European Premiere of Simon Stone’s Elsinore , starring Andrew Scott, and close with the UK Premiere of Jesse Eisenberg’s The Debut . Other highlight titles include Ava DuVernay’s 14th, which will screen in the festival’s Special Presentations strand. The film details how the tenets of the 14th Amendment, ratified post-Civil War, are now under systematic attack. Other titles in the Special Presentations strand include a new restoration of Michael Powell and Emeric Pressburger’s Gone To Earth and The Trip To The Northern Lights , the latest instalment in Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon’s travel comedy series. Michael Winterbottom has directed the series. NEW ADDITIONS TO THE PROGRAMME: ARTIFICIAL Sunday 11 October 21:00 and Friday 16 October 11:30 at the Southbank Centre’s Royal Festival Hall, Thursday 15 October 15:30 at Vue West End Director Luca Guadagnino. Screenwriter Simon Rich. Andrew Garfield, Yura Borisov, Monica Barbaro, Cooper Hoffman, Jason Schwartzman, Chris O’Dowd with Ike Barinholtz and Mark Rylance. USA-Italy 2026. 140min. Courtesy of NEON. Language English Luca Guadagnino returns to the Festival with his fascinating and of-the-moment origin story of Open AI and its co-founder, Sam Altman. Artificial homes in on the rise of Open AI and the tumultuous period that saw Altman ousted as CEO of his own company. Andrew Garfield has rarely been better in his portrayal of the tech entrepreneur, with an impressive cast joining him. Writer Simon Rich and Guadagnino ( Queer , LFF 2024; After the Hunt , LFF 2025) centre the human drama and ethical conundrums facing the creators of this life-changing technology. Screening as part of our GALA strand. CAMERON WINTER AT CARNEGIE HALL Wednesday 7 October 18:30 at Prince Charles Cinema and Thursday 8 October 15:00 at BFI Southbank Director Paul Thomas Anderson. With Cameron Winter. USA 2026. 71 min. Courtesy of MUBI. Language English. ‘One Battle After Another’ director Paul Thomas Anderson creates an intimate document of Geese frontman Cameron Winter’s solo piano performance at the legendary New York concert hall. In December 2025, Paul Thomas Anderson collaborated with fellow filmmaker Benny Safdie on a multi-perspective and multi-format recording of Winter’s solo performance. The warm hues capture the feeling in the room, including audience reactions, to create an immersive cinematic experience for those of us who couldn’t be there. It’s a rapturous celebration of live performance, whose appeal should reach far beyond the band and Winter’s existing fan base. Screening as part of our CREATE strand. EVEREST: THE OTHER SIDE Saturday 10 October 12:45 at Vue West End and Tuesday 13 October 18:20 at BFI Southbank Director Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi, Jimmy Chin. With Jim Morrison, Hilaree Nelson. USA 2026.113min. Courtesy of Walt Disney Studios. Language English This intimate portrait from the directors of Oscar winner Free Solo follows a mountaineering couple with a shared passion and ambition for the near-impossible. Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin once again show their passion for individuals who push themselves to the limits of human endurance. Jim Morrison and Hilaree Nelson share a dream of becoming the first to successfully climb up and ski down the north face of Everest – a feat that prompts concern among friends and family. The resulting film is a compelling and moving portrait of perseverance. Screening as part of our JOURNEY strand. JOY OF JOYS Sunday 11 October 13:45 Vue West End Director Jonathan Glazer. With Olivia Rodrigo, Arctic Monkeys. UK 2026. 38min. With some English subtitles Devised by Mica Levi and Jonathan Glazer, and seen through young eyes, Joy of Joys transforms the making of War Child’s record HELP(2) into something tender and playful. At Abbey Road, London schoolchildren film recording sessions with artists including Olivia Rodrigo, Arctic Monkeys and Jarvis Cocker – their small digital cameras capturing the music with curiosity and wonder. Meanwhile, children in Gaza, Sudan, Ukraine and Yemen record fragments of their daily lives. Moving between these images, the film finds in music a form of witness and refuge, and in childhood, a spirit of play and joy that persists amid catastrophe. Screening as part of our CREATE strand. PRIMETIME Sunday 11 October 18:00 at BFI IMAX Director Lance Oppenheim. Screenwriter Ajon Singh. With Robert Pattinson, Merritt Wever, and Anna Faris. USA 2026. 107min. Courtesy of A24. Language English. Contains Flashing images. Robert Pattinson continues his run of astonishing 2026 performances as he portrays the To Catch a Predator presenter Chris Hansen in this vivid and propulsive drama. It’s 2006 and despite its unconventional methods, To Catch a Predator is a US TV hit. When executives decide to move the show to a primetime slot, Hansen and his production team must up the ante to keep their audience, no matter the cost. Merritt Weaver and Skyler Gisondo also impress in this absorbing narrative feature debut from documentary filmmaker Lance Oppenheim. Screening as part of our THRILL strand. MISTY GREEN Monday 12 October 18:30 at Vue West End and Sunday 18 October 18:15 at BFI Southbank Director-Screenwriter Chris Rock. With Rosalind Eleazar, Adam Driver, Daniel Kaluuya USA 2026. 104min. Courtesy of A24 Films. Language English. Contains flashing images Chris Rock turns his eye to contemporary Hollywood in this biting comedy, in which a washed-up actress attempts to turn her life around in the course of a week. Misty Green used to be a somebody. These days, she’s barely scraping by. But when an old acquaintance re-enters her life, it looks like she might finally have the chance to start afresh. However, when the biggest obstacle is yourself, rebooting your life is not always so easy. Rosalind Eleazar is magnetic as Misty, and is joined by an all-star cast including Rock, Daniel Kaluuya and Adam Driver. Screening as part of our JOURNEY strand. INHERIT Friday 9 October 20:50 at Curzon Soho and Saturday 10 October 11:10 at Prince Charles Cinema Director Banjong Pisanthanakun. Screenwriter Banjong Pisanthanakun, Thamsatid Charoenrittichai, Chantavit Dhanasevi. With Davika Hoorne, Baipor Thitiya Jirapornsilp, Sinjai Plengpanich. Thailand 2026. 129min. Courtesy of Barunson E&A. Language Thai. A rich Thai family falls apart with the arrival of a distant relative in Banjong Pisanthanakun’s (The Medium, LFF 2021) gripping and unpredictable new horror. Grandma Woranart is full of surprises. She claims to be 80 but has the face of a beautiful young woman. That turns out to be the tip of the iceberg, as family secrets are gradually revealed, and it becomes all too apparent that something sinister lurks inside this seemingly benign relative. Featuring a magnetic performance by Davika Hoorne (A Useful Ghost), Inherit thrills as much as it chills. Screening this film as part of our CULT strand. JAVIER BARDEM SCREEN TALK Sunday 11 October 10:30 at Curzon Soho We welcome Javier Bardem to the Festival, whose Screen Talk accompanies his stunning performances in Gala entries The Beloved and Bunker. One of the most accomplished actors of his generation, Javier Bardem first gained attention with roles in Bigas Luna’s Jamón Jamón and Golden Balls. He followed it with an outstanding performance in Pedro Almodóvar’s thriller, Live Flesh. Further acclaim and international roles followed, with lead performances in Julian Schnabel’s Before Night Falls, for which he received his first Academy Award nomination, and John Malkovich’s The Dancer Upstairs, as well as a scene-stealing cameo in Michael Mann’s Collateral. His moving performance in Alejandro Amenábar’s The Sea Inside saw him win the fourth of his seven Goya awards, while his portrayal of a ruthless, sociopathic killer in the Coen Brothers’ No Country for Old Men brought him an Oscar, BAFTA and Golden Globe. He changed tack to play the charming object of desire for two American tourists in Vicky Cristina Barcelona, and followed it with a Cannes-winning performance as a dying man haunted by ghosts from the past in Alejandro González Iñárritu’s emotionally raw Biutiful. Bardem received another Oscar and Golden Globe nomination for his role in Aaron Sorkin’s Being The Ricardos, and was Emmy, SAG and Golden Globe-nominated as José Menendez in Monsters: The Lyle and Erik Menendez Story. Over the last two decades, Javier Bardem has worked with Terrence Malick, Sam Mendes, Ridley Scott, Darren Aronofsky, Ryan Murphy, Josph Kosinski, and Denis Villeneuve. He played Silva, one of the most captivating Bond villains, in Skyfall, was terrifying as Max Cady in the serial adaptation of Cape Fear and will return to our screens in December as Stilgar in the much-anticipated third part of the Dune trilogy. ROBERT EGGERS SCREEN TALK Sunday 11 October, 17:30 VUE West End In advance of the New Years Day 2027 opening of Werwulf, we welcome writer-director-producer Robert Eggers to this Screen Talk to discuss his career. A master storyteller whose five features all unfold before the 20th century and revel in a world of myths, legends, folk tales and gothic atmosphere, Robert Eggers is one of the 21st century’s most distinctive filmmakers. Initially displaying an interest in theatre – where his vision for Nosferatu first began – he soon moved from experimental and street theatre to film, developing the story for his feature debut The Witch. Immersing himself in the early 17th century, he wrote a script with dialogue and a dialect as close to that era as he could achieve – an element of his process that would continue through all his subsequent work. The Witch proved an outlier among contemporary horror films and paved the way for his visually striking and boldly original sophomore feature, The Lighthouse. That saw Willem Dafoe and Robert Pattinson as two 19th-century lighthouse keepers gradually driven mad. The Northman, Robert Eggers’ first collaboration with Icelandic novelist Sjón, marked a significant increase in scale, as it detailed a Viking warrior’s trail of destruction as he avenges his murdered father. No less ambitious, Eggers’ take on F.W. Murnau’s Nosferatu is a gruesomely beautiful tale of tortured love and bloodlust, receiving four Oscar® and five BAFTA nominations. He returns with his most visceral and haunting experience yet, upcoming Werwulf, once again co-written with Sjón, a harrowing tale of devotion, damnation and the devil within. We welcome him to this Screen Talk to discuss these films and his vision of the world. title: Ellen Burstyn Cries as She Gets Venice Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement: ‘It’s One Thing to Win an Oscar, Tony or Emmy — All of Which I’ve Won. But This Is a Lot’
full_text: Sep 7, 2026 6:50am PT Ellen Burstyn Cries as She Gets Venice Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement: ‘It’s One Thing to Win an Oscar, Tony or Emmy — All of Which I’ve Won. But This Is a Lot’ By Rebecca Rubin Plus Icon Rebecca Rubin Senior Film and Media Reporter rebeccaarubin Latest ‘Possible Love’ Cast Sobs as Lee Chang-dong’s Epic Embraced at Venice With 6-Minute Standing Ovation 21 hours ago Box Office: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Remains No. 1 in Sixth Weekend, Nears ‘Avengers: Endgame’ All-Time Domestic Record 21 hours ago Robert Pattinson Kisses Suki Waterhouse as ‘Primetime’ Rocks Venice With 7-Minute Standing Ovation 2 days ago See All Getty Images Maggie Gyllenhaal delivered a message on behalf of Ellen Burstyn before the 93-year-old acting legend took the stage at the Venice Film Festival to receive the prestigious Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement. “Ellen asked me to let you know that she recently took a fall,” Gyllenhaal said from the podium. “She’s OK, but she is moving more slowly — which is fine because it’ll give us more time to clap.” Related Stories ‘The Idiot(s)’ Review: Dostoevsky Is an Endearing Drunken Fool in This Rambunctious, Tonally Off-Kilter Two-Hander How John Malkovich’s 30-Year Oscar Drought Could Finally End With ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Indeed, the room burst into applause as Burstyn, clad in a vibrant yellow gown, sauntered onto the stage with a walker. Burstyn cried and wiped away her tears with a tissue as she was greeted with a heartfelt, minutes-long standing ovation. Popular on Variety “You’re making me cry!” she said, which did little to stop the enthusiastic applause. “You’re overwhelming me, you know! I don’t know how to recover from that generous greeting.” Burstyn has achieved a lot in her seven-decade career in Hollywood, which she was quick to remind the crowd, but she puts the Venice award among the top honors. “You can’t imagine how meaningful this is to me It’s one thing to win an Oscar, a Tony or an Emmy — all of which I’ve won,” she said. “But this … it’s a lot.” Since she learned she’d receive the Golden Lion, she said, she’s been reflecting on her life — and what it means to get a career tribute. “At 93, it means you have a far about of lifetime to look back on,” she said. “I thought, maybe it’s not just a record of what you’ve accomplished, but what you’ve learned.” During her speech, she recalled that while shooting Martin Scorsese’s 1974 drama “Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore,” she was required to film a nighttime driving scene while the director and the cinematographer were blocking her view of the street. “I couldn’t see the side of the road; I could go off and kill all of us,” Burstyn said. “But then I noticed, this is a two-way road. There’s a white line in the middle of the road, and I can see that. So all I have to do is look up to the left, and follow the white line. And that’s how I managed to not kill Martin Scorsese.” She then drew a parallel between the funny story and the fraught state of the U.S. right now, saying: “I wanted to close out saying how deeply appreciative I am of this Golden Lion and I hope — no, pray — that my own country will find its own white line.” Burstyn was awarded the Golden Lion on Monday afternoon during the premiere of Gyllenhaal’s short film “Flesh Impact.” Taika Waititi, Pamela Anderson and Murray Bartlett, her co-stars in “Place to Be,” a comedic drama that premieres Wednesday on the Lido, attended the ceremony. The trio were among the first to lead another standing ovation when Burstyn exited the stage and went to sit in the audience. Dedicated to Marilyn Monroe on what would be her 100th birthday, the 20-minute-long “Flesh Impact” portrays Dakota Johnson as the actress at the height of her fame and Burstyn as the version of Monroe the world never got to see. The star died on Aug. 4, 1962 at age 36 from an acute barbiturate overdose. The short’s title, “Flesh Impact,” comes from a phrase once used to describe the aura of Monroe — “that she looked so real and luminous on camera that viewers felt they could touch her through the screen,” according to the synopsis. Prior to the ceremony, Burstyn sat on Monday morning for a press conference and spoke about a fleeting encounter with Monroe way back when. “We never met. We saw each other once. We went to a nightclub, and she was sitting across from me,” Burstyn recalled. “And of course, I was enchanted by just looking at her. She was such a magical creature. And then she looked at me and nodded at me. And I was very early in my career, and I thought, was I just recognized by Marilyn Monroe?” She had another connection to Monroe, through Ralph Roberts, an actor-turned-masseur to the stars. “Ralph Roberts, who had been Marilyn’s masseur, and not only that, but her confidant, he had lots of stories to tell me about Marilyn,” Burstyn said. “So I used to get my massages and hear Marilyn’s stories. My favorite one was that her whole persona was a construction.” Burstyn was asked if she had any other memorable encounters with other Hollywood luminaries, to which she responded, “When I met Marlon Brando briefly, and I almost fainted. That was pretty spectacular.” Then, she cracked, “I can’t think of anyone else — it mustn’t have impressed me too much.” She also recalled the early career advice she received from Bette Davis, who was 24 years her senior. “I had just become known,” Burstyn said. “I was new, but famous. I met [Davis] and she said, ‘Let me tell you one thing, honey. At the beginning of your illustrious career, the only thing that’s important is your work. Anybody that tries to get in the way of you and your work, they’re your enemy. You know what you say to them? ‘You are my enemy.’ I said, “Thank you, Mrs. Davis…” Burstyn has two movies at Venice, the other being Kornél Mundruczó’s quirky drama “Place to Be,” which premieres on Wednesday. She stars in “Place to Be” alongside Waititi, Anderson, Édgar Ramírez, Lena Waithe and Bartlett. Mundruczó and Burstyn previously collaborated on “Pieces of a Woman,” which premiered on the Lido in 2020. Burstyn, who is still acting as a nonagenarian, described her rationale for saying “yes” to projects. “When I get a script, I sit down and read it — and if it makes me laugh, that’s good. If it makes me cry, that’s good. If it makes me laugh and cry, that’s terrific,” she said. “By the time I finish the script, I have to feel moved in some way to say, ‘I want to do this.'” As Burstyn mentioned in her Golden Lion Speech, she is one of the few performers to achieve the Triple Crown of Acting, earning an Oscar for “Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore” and a Tony for “Same Time, Next Year” in 1975, and two Emmys for “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” and “Political Animals” in 2009 and 2013, respectively. Over her 60-year career in Hollywood, Burstyn has received dozens of nominations for films and television shows including “The Exorcist,” “The Last Picture Show,” “Requiem for a Dream” and “House of Cards.” Burstyn believes roles for women in entertainment have changed “enormously” over the decades. She added that although the industry is “not quite 50-50” in terms of parity, “they’re close.” “When I first started working, which was 150 years ago, there were no women on set. No women crew. No women directing. It was all men,” she said. “If a woman was on set, it meant she was an actress. And then slowly, thanks to blessed Gloria Steinem, who just died, the consciousness started to be changed.” Starz’s U.K.-Set Boxing Crime Drama ‘Fightland’ Is a Knockout: TV Review Loading comments... title: Streaming Is Raising Prices Faster Than Cable Ever Did
full_text: × Skip to main content By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All September 7, 2026 6:05am Illustrated by Brian Taylor Yup, you’re getting screwed. The cost to simply watch new TV shows is up — way up — with streaming services delivering one wearisome price shock after another that rival the worst of the cable and satellite price hikes of yesteryear. Since 2022, streaming prices have risen more than three times as much as inflation (which is also too high). Behold some not-so-fun facts: · The price of Apple TV has tripled. The streamer launched at just $4.99 in 2019. It’s jumped 200 percent despite having the thinnest library — in terms of quantity, at least — of the major streamers. · Disney+ is right behind Apple TV. The service launched at $6.99 with no ads in 2019 and has since jumped to $11.99 with ads — or pay a whopping 172 percent more than its launch price. · Paramount+ ’s cheapest tier is up 80 percent in five years. Netflix Premium is up 125 percent since 2013. · If you want all eight major streamers without ads or bundle commitments, it’ll cost you about $151 a month. Four years ago, the comparable lineup cost about $90. So you thought you cut the cord, but now you probably have four, five or six cords — and each is auto-drafting from your bank account so you can keep watching Love Island and Tulsa King . The outlier here is HBO Max, having only climbed 23 percent over six years. HBO has been priced as a premium product for decades, however, and launched its streaming service in 2020 at a higher price point than the other services. And these numbers hide some recent drama. Apple TV went up 50 percent just in the past year. Peacock’s tiers likewise leapt about 50 percent. (It’s a bit wild that HBO Premium is only $3 more than Peacock Premium Plus, especially when the former gives you dragons and Hogwarts and the latter offers The Miniature Wife and Married at First Sight. ) Over the course of the past 12 months, streaming rates have collectively risen 11.8 percent. The biggest year of increase was 2023, when the streamers shot up an average of 17.7 percent. A Hollywood Reporter analysis of Bureau of Labor Statistics data shows cable and satellite prices, by comparison, rose an annual average of 3.9 percent — excluding a deregulation surge of the late 1980s, when the index peaked at 14 percent. But that was a seismic shift provoked by a federal intervention rather than, say, because Widow’s Bay is a good show, or “we’re pretty sure we can get away with this.” It’s worth pointing out that streaming hikes have wildly outpaced inflation — even with inflation wildly outpacing what should be inflation. Consumer prices have climbed an average of 3.84 percent annually since 2019, double the Federal Reserve’s 2 percent target. That number might still seem small, but it’s added up to a 33 percent increase in the cost of consumer living, which is why everything besides a Costco hot dog has gotten noticeably more expensive. This is also why streaming price hikes are such a gut punch — annual bumps of 10 or 15 percent compound fast. At this point, you might be wondering: Does this mean cable TV is now a better deal by comparison? Not at all, not unless you’re a massive sports fan or are really into the Hallmark Channel (hey, My Christmas Cowboy debuts in December). Fully loaded bundles from the likes of Spectrum and DirecTV cost north of $170. So what’s the solution? Just quietly suffer? Yes — in one way or another. You could do what your uncle commenting on this story on Facebook will suggest (perhaps in all caps): Buy an over-the-air antenna for $25 and tune into whatever the broadcast gods are willing to give you. But that way lies entertainment despair. Our TV past wasn’t actually better — you were just younger, so everything seemed better. The best hack comes courtesy of Gen Z, who have reportedly embraced streaming cycling. You

She’d been dating Luke Gulbranson, then a castmember on Summer House , Bravo’s long-running series about a group of attractive young New Yorkers who spend their weekends drinking, hooking up and occasionally screaming at each other in the Hamptons. In 2020, Gulbranson invited her to join him in the house for season five. She never really left. Six years later, Miller has become one of Bravo’s more recognizable faces, parlaying Summer House into appearances on Winter House and The Traitors , then the Love Island hosting job and now Dancing With the Stars . She’d been trying to land that last one for a while. “I have talked to the Dancing With the Stars team for the past two years,” she says. “So when they wanted to have a call this year, I was like, ‘Absolutely, let’s do our yearly call because I’m obviously trying to be on the show.’” This time, the answer was yes. And as it happens, DWTS may be the one reality show Miller has been inadvertently preparing for most of her life. Long before the ICU or Bravo, she studied ballet, jazz and hip-hop. Miller calls herself “the show pony of my family” and remembers constantly staging homemade music videos for her grandmother, who took her to see Alvin Ailey performances. “I was always choreographing a music video for my grandmother to watch. Poor her — I mean, she would be proud of me picking up a pencil, literally anything,” Miller says. “[ DWTS ] is really a full-circle moment, coming back to my dancing roots and being able to perform on a stage this big.” Of course, there is a downside to spending six years turning your life into television: Eventually, your life becomes television. Miller learned that rather spectacularly this spring. She had been romantically involved with fellow Summer House castmember West Wilson when Wilson and Amanda Batula — one of Miller’s closest friends on the reality series — announced they were together. The very public betrayal left Miller wondering whether she wanted to return for season 11 and spend another summer under the same roof with the people involved. Wilson and Batula subsequently exited, while Miller stayed. “I definitely was very much on the fence about coming back to Summer House , full disclosure,” she says. But walking away would also have meant letting what happened determine what she did next. “I also felt like I’ve been in that house since I was 24, and these are my friends. Why wouldn’t I spend my summer how I’ve been spending my summer?” Miller says. “And to let a situation dictate where I’m going to be, I wasn’t willing to do that.” Wiederhoeft top, skirt; Marie Mas jewelry. Photographed by Nina Westervelt So she went back. And now, with Dancing With the Stars about to start, Miller is heading into yet another reality show — albeit one where, for once, all the drama is supposed to happen on the dance floor, but somehow always makes its way online. Reality TV can be a breeding ground for negativity, on- and off-screen. Miller has experience navigating the viciousness that can be the Bravo audiences, but she also was faced with criticism this summer from Love Island fans for her Aftersun hosting style. Dancing With the Stars fans are no angels either, and oftentimes, viewers’ pessimism centers mainly around a celebrity’s dance capabilities. Being judged on by performance rather than personality on a reality show “will be a whole different experience” for Miller. She also knows that’s “part of the experience” of Dancing With the Stars , but it won’t define her time on the series. “I don’t think you’re ever really prepared for the fandom, but I’ve been warmed up with the Bravo crowd, and honestly, even the Love Island fans, because they are a whole type of breed,” Miller says. “I’d like to say that I’m a little accustomed to fan feedback, and that’s great. We welcome it. Here’s the thing: You say thank you when you need to, and put your head down when you also need to.” Miller “love[s] to hear” viewer’s opinions, because “sometimes you can’t take their input and kind of tweak it and put your own spin on things.” But part of staying in the unscripted business is not paying mind to that negativity. “I don’t really ride the waves of what the fan response is typically, and that’s, a lot of times, how I get through it on Summer House and even Love Island ,” she says. “I like to see what everyone has to say, and I love that people will be talking about it. And hopefully, they’re nice. You just pray.” On Summer House , Miller knows she’s known for lounging in bed, so much so that her friend group was dubbed “Bed Bugs.” But on Dancing With the Stars , she’s ready to show off her competitive side. “I know part of my persona is being horizontal and in the bed, so people are really going to see me out of the bed,” Miller says. “People can only call me lazy for so much longer.” Much of Miller’s career has been dominated by reality TV. Her heart and soul are concentrated on Dancing With the Stars right now, but that doesn’t mean she’s not thinking ahead about a career away from cameras. “My wheels are always turning in terms of where I want to land and what would make sense for me as a landing pad post-reality TV. Because look, I’ll be honest, I’m not the reality TV girl that’s gonna get married on TV and have my kids on TV,” Miller admits. “The chances of that happening are slim to none. I’m a Capricorn. I’m always thinking five years ahead. But at this point in time, at this juncture, I’m not quite sure. I’m still figuring that out.” Photographed by Nina Westervelt This story appears in the Sept. 9 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

title: How a Sweet, Horny Hockey Show Rewrote the Rules of Independent TV
full_text: × Skip to main content (L to R): Accent Aigu co-founders Brendan Brady, Jacob Tierney Ted Belton The story of Accent Aigu Entertainment, the Canadian production company behind 2026’s global TV breakout Heated Rivalry , began with a love story — between two dogs. Jacob Tierney was directing and showrunning on Letterkenny , the cult comedy he co-created with Jared Keeso, which aired on Crave in Canada and Hulu in the U.S. Brendan Brady had been brought on as a line producer. Both Tierney and Brady had dogs: Graham, a Lab/hound mutt, and Murphy, a black Labradoodle. “Murphy’s a boy. Graham is a girl. I know that’s confusing, but that’s crucial,” says Tierney. “We brought them together, and our dogs fell in love. That’s our meet-cute. For the next season, when we came back to do more Letterkenny , they got us a place where we shared a backyard so the dogs could play together.” Related Stories Movies Lee Chang-dong's 'Possible Love' Emerges as Venice Film Festival Sensation Movies Venice's Lone Female Competition Director May el-Toukhy on Gender Gap: "I've Never Heard a Female Director Being Called a Genius" “That was basically our lake house,” jokes Brady, referencing a much-memed scene from the season one finale of Heated Rivalry . “We decided to take it to the next level.” In 2023, after finishing Letterkenny and working on the first two seasons of its spinoff, Shoresy , Tierney and Brady left to launch Accent Aigu Entertainment. (The name, a tongue-in-cheek reference to Tierney’s Quebecois Francophone roots, was chosen “after several libations,” Brady admits.) The plan was to make independent TV in a new way that was both faster and cheaper without sacrificing creative vision. Cutting-edge TV on a budget. “The cost-effective element was what we were really excited about,” Brady says. “With Jacob’s amazing ability as a director and my experience as a line producer, we understood we could change the way production is made.” Three years and one low-budget Canadian queer hockey romance later, Tierney and Brady are more than just the flavor of the moment. Accent Aigu Entertainment stands as a model for something the international TV business is scrambling to figure out: how to make premium, globally competitive scripted television when the big streamers are no longer writing blank checks for it. Tierney and Brady applied their cost-saving strategies on the low-budget Letterkenny to Heated Rivalry. Lindsay Sarazin/Hulu The Accent Aigu method was honed on Letterkenny and its legendarily tight shoots. “People talk about how low-budget Heated Rivalry was,” notes Tierney, “but we shot six episodes of Letterkenny season one in 18 days. As a director-showrunner, my task was to create an aesthetic where we could do that and have it still be creative and visually appealing.” It starts with the scripts. On Letterkenny , Tierney and Keeso wrote “long scenes that were very still, not a lot of entrances and exits. Not a lot of movement,” says Tierney. “You can cover that in an aesthetically pleasing way so that the limitations turn into a choice. It’s a big master, you cover the close-ups, and then you’re done. Eight pages, eight minutes of the show, in like an hour and a half.” Hudson Williams, who plays Shane Hollander on Heated Rivalry, recalls the same approach on that show. “Jacob would use these long ‘oners,’ which are technically harder to achieve but if successful do save time over standard coverage,” he says. “They also look more cinematic than most TV shows.” The standard model of making television involves having multiple directors shoot each season, hired guns who come in to do one or two episodes each. Accent Aigu likes to lock in one or two directors for a whole season. (Tierney directed all six episodes of Heated Rivalry season one and will direct all of season two.) “The benefits are that you are not shooting blocks of TV, going back to the same locations over and over, which is how things are normally done,” says Tierney. “We shoot more like an independent film, location for location.” (L to R): Heated Rivalry stars Connor Storrie, Hudson Williams, director Jacob Tierney, producer Brendan Brady on the set of season 1. Sabrina-Lantos Adds Brady, “If you have an actor who you only need in one location or two locations, you can get them in for a day or two, as opposed to having them come in once a week for five weeks. It’s a model —especially in the Canadian system where budgets are restricted — that’s a very smart way to get television made. An independent film model for independent TV.” The original plan was to apply the Accent Aigu model to comedy. Then Tierney, who during the pandemic had become a voracious audiobook listener, discovered the hockey-romance subgenre and Rachel Reid’s Game Changers novels. The sweet and smutty tales involving same-sex romances between professional hockey players were below the radar of most television producers, but they were exploding on BookTok and had a fiercely devoted fan base. Tierney slid into Reid’s Instagram DMs and asked if anyone had optioned the rights. Nobody had, and Reid, a Letterkenny fan, was in. Jacob Tierney and Brendan Brady honed their “quality TV on a budget” style on cult Canadian sitcom Letterkenny . Courtesy of Lindsay Sarazin/Hulu Tierney adapted Reid’s second novel, Heated Rivalry , which follows two Major League Hockey stars, Canadian Shane Hollander (Williams) and Russian Ilya Rozanov (Connor Storrie) — fictional stand-ins for actual on-ice rivals Sidney Crosby and Alexander Ovechkin — who are drawn together into an intense, sweaty love affair. Tierney wrote the script on spec and pitched it to Bell Media, the owner of Crave, Letterkenny ‘s home network. Following the success of Bridgerton and The Summer I Turned Pretty , he knew Bell Media was looking for a romance series. But Heated Rivalry , with its queer storylines and graphic sex, felt risky — especially for Bell, which in addition to being the home of HBO in Canada, is the home of hockey broadcasting. “I read the first script and thought, ‘This is going to be special — [either] an insane flop or a real thing,’ ” Justin Stockman, vp content development and programming at Bell Media, told the Toronto Star . “Reading the second episode, I was sure I was going to get fired because it’s probably the most racy of all the episodes. But I thought, ‘This is worth getting fired over.’ “ Produced for roughly CA $3 million (about $2.2 million) an episode — a fraction of comparable HBO-level drama budgets — Heated Rivalry shot for 36 days in and around Toronto and Hamilton in spring 2025, doubling Ontario soundstages for Moscow, New York and a Las Vegas hotel room. The show leaned in on Accent Aigu’s playbook of long, unbroken takes and efficient indie film-style production. (L to R): Jacob Tierney and Brendan Brady share a laugh on the set Heated Rivalry. Sabrina-Lantos “Their approach was always, ‘Test it with less, and if it’s not enough, do more,’ ” Williams recalls. “In episode two, there’s the ice cream scene [set in Sochi, Russia]. At first it was just some chairs and tables on the volume stage, with the LED volume doing everything else. [But] it looked so fake that they scrapped the shoot. When we came back, they’d built a cafe and used longer lenses to make the background more out of focus. They tried less, and when it didn’t work, they added more.” Adds Storrie: “They prioritized the people, the connection and the world-building over having millions of resources. They played to their strengths — they were fast, precise and prepared.” On set, Brady kept morale up by periodically wandering into tense scenes in character as an invented superfan of Shane and Ilya. “He’d show up in the shower scene,” says Williams. “He’d do this dumb-jock-guy voice and say something like, ‘Hell yeah, fellas, I’m feeling it too!’ in relation to a certain excited appendage.” Tierney and Brady’s bet with Heated Rivalry was the old indie adage of producing for an underserved audience. In this case, that meant both queer fans hungry for a sexy romance story that doesn’t end in tragedy, and the large female demographic, the “wine mums” who make up the core contingent of Reid’s readership. “What we knew from the fans of the [ Heated Rivalry ] books is that they’re evangelical,” says Tierney. “They knock on doors, they tell their friends. They spread the good news online and on social media.” The show was designed to serve the superfans. Instead of a conventional will-they-or-won’t-they relationship drama, Tierney follows the books and gets straight to the sex. The approach annoyed some critics, but the fans loved it. When the first steamy 90-second trailer of the show dropped late last year, it exploded online, spawning a thousand TikTok memes. They knew they had something special. Connor Storie and Hudson Williams in Heated Rivalry. Courtesy of HBO Max/Photo Illustration by The Sporting Press Taking the series global, however, was a different challenge. Tierney and Brady held the IP for the show and had presold Canadian rights to Bell, so Heated Rivalry was less attractive for the global streamers — Netflix, Amazon or Apple — which like to buy all rights worldwide. And, outside Canada, few networks saw the commercial appeal of a horny hockey show featuring a lot of gay sex. “We were given a comically low offer, like $200,000,” says Tierney. “It was either 200 grand an episode or 200 grand for all six. For the world! And we’d have to pay for the dubbing and subtitles. Basically, it would have cost us to do the deal.” The show was saved by a buyer with a different appetite: HBO, which acquires territory by territory rather than insisting on the whole world. Jason Butler, HBO and HBO Max senior vp global content planning and programming, was an early booster and brought Heated Rivalry to HBO CEO Casey Bloys, who snatched it up for the main U.S. network as well as Australia. HBO would later take the show for most of Europe and Asia, with separate deals for Sky in the U.K., Movistar Plus+ in Spain and Neon in New Zealand. When the U.S. and Australia deals were finalized, HBO decided to go day-and-date with the Canadian premiere — with three weeks’ notice. “We could not believe the level of speed we were dealing with,” Brady says. “Between Nov. 1, when the show premiered, to Dec. 26, we were literally still finishing episodes.” “I was in the editing room, saying, ‘That music cue is wrong,’ while things are exploding online around the show,” Tierney recalls. “Ten days after the finale aired, we were at the Golden Globes party.” The explosion, when it came, was fast and total. Heated Rivalry was Crave’s biggest original series debut on record, with viewership up nearly 400 percent in its first week; a second-season renewal followed within days. On HBO Max, the show reached an average of 10.6 million viewers per episode in the U.S., making it the platform’s most watched acquired scripted series in history. Streaming minutes grew from roughly 30 million in its first week to more than 300 million by the season finale. Weeks after Heated Rivalry premiered, Storrie and Williams were presenting at the Golden Globes. Rich Polk/2026GG “When we acquired it, I had some sense that it would make some noise,” Bloys tells THR . “But over the course of two to three weeks, it was just steady growth. It was growing on the platform, growing online, growing in media … like a hockey stick, you know, up and to the right.” (Or just like, Brendan and Tierney might add, an accent aigu .) “I think what people responded to is the combination of the sex and the sweetness; I can’t think of another show that has that combination,” says Bloys. “There’s a sweetness to the story of Hudson and Connor, seeing them go from being waiters to walking red carpets in designer clothing … these sorts of stories don’t happen all the time.” If there’s a single lesson Accent Aigu wants the industry to take from all this, it’s about paying attention, early and seriously, to underserved audiences who are already organizing themselves online. “For years, TV executives have assumed certain genres only appeal to niche audiences,” says Brady. “What’s happening here proves otherwise.” Accent Aigu has since formalized its growth spurt into an actual company: Tierney and Brady, formerly co-presidents, have become chief creative officer and CEO, respectively, adding an entire C-suite, including Jayme Alter Wilson as president and Craig Merritt as CFO, with Lori Fischburg as the new head of production and Liane Cunje as development executive and producer. It’s built to scale up a slate rather than shepherd a single show. Heated Rivalry’ s Christina Chang, Brady, Robbie G.K., Tierney and Nadine Bhabha at the 2026 GLAAD Media Awards. Vivien Killilea/Getty Images The global success of Heated Rivalry , Tierney admits, “is not necessarily replicable.” What is, he argues, is the Accent Aigu approach of trusting a genuinely weird, specific creative vision and producing for the most passionate fans. “If you want to break through the noise, trust somebody to do something weird,” he says. “Whether it’s Taylor Sheridan or the guy that created Squid Game in South Korea, or Richard Gadd with Baby Reindeer or us with Heated Rivalry . If you let a weird person do a weird thing, people might pay attention to it. You might break through the noise and get that big return.” If Heated Rivalry has a lesson for executives or the industry writ large, that’s it, Tierney says. “It’s definitely not, ‘Let’s do more hockey shows.’ “ This story appeared in the Sept. 2 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

title: ‘Imperium’ Review: Sergei Loznitsa Brings Together Nearly Three Hours of Italian Footage From the Early 1970s Covering the Vastness of the USSR
full_text: Sep 7, 2026 5:15am PT ‘Imperium’ Review: Sergei Loznitsa Brings Together Nearly Three Hours of Italian Footage From the Early 1970s Covering the Vastness of the USSR Journeying from Moscow to the Soviet Far East and then back west, this sprawling documentary shows a multicultural nation stubbornly resistant to Politburo attempts at homogeneity. By Jay Weissberg Plus Icon Jay Weissberg Latest ‘It Will Happen Tonight’ Review: Louis Garrel and Jasmine Trinca Follow Each Other Through the Years In a Light and Predictable Romcom 2 days ago ‘The City of the Living’ Review: A Superbly Acted and Heartbreakingly Real Story Based on a Real Event That Shook Rome to Its Core 3 days ago ‘Al Baraneya’ Review: Cinema Verité Doesn’t Get More Naturalistic Than Egyptian Director Ashgan El-Hamus’ Impressive Debut 3 days ago See All Essential Filmproduktion, Kino Produzioni, Société Parisienne de Production, Studio Uljana Kim In the early 1970s, Italian film crews spread out across the USSR, capturing a vast, multicultural empire few had ever seen in such diversity. From urban commuters to village fêtes, Baku trawlers to Siberian reindeer herders, the cameramen aimed to capture the Soviet polity at a time when Westerners had a gray, monolithic image of what lay behind the Iron Curtain. Granted official permission, they managed to resist any push towards propaganda, even finding ways to slyly critique a system that proclaimed regional autonomy but controlled everything from the Kremlin. While planned as a monumental, multi-chapter TV series, only a few episodes wound up being broadcast on Italian TV, just once, following which the endeavor lay forgotten in the archives. If ever there was a project for Sergei Loznitsa , this was it. Related Stories Nathan Fielder Drops Weird Trailer for Secret Elizabeth Holmes Doc ‘You Can See Everything’ Meet Topic, the Indie Studio Dominating the Festival Circuit With ‘The Debut,’ ‘Club Kid,’ ‘Wicker’ In “ Imperium ,” working with 60 hours of 16mm, the master documentarian organizes this journey along geographic lines, starting in Moscow and heading east, then doubling back through “the Stans” and the Baltic republics until ending in what was then Leningrad. As with Loznitsa’s past films of this type, some snippets of conversation and music have been added, but otherwise the footage has simply been restored and edited together. What’s revealed is an immense state whose distinct regions still managed to hold onto unique traditions, notwithstanding an incessant centralized proclamation of unity. Popular on Variety While “Imperium” can be engrossing, its nearly three-hour running time is felt more than in Loznitsa masterpieces like “Maidan” and “State Funeral.” Perhaps that’s because in those films, one feels the force of history pushing us forward, inexorably heading to a watershed moment whose impact continues to resonate across the decades. With “Imperium,” the motivation is clear yet the concept is more diffuse. It’s also a film which will likely resonate best with those of us old enough to recall how the Soviet Union was discussed in the West at the time, a decade before Ronald Reagan’s “Evil Empire” remark — which simply gave a reductivist Star Wars moniker to the anti-communist propaganda suffusing American-driven global discourse since the end of the Second World War. For Loznitsa, of course, his interest is inside the country rather than how it was perceived from abroad, though it will be impossible for most audiences to separate the two. The film kicks off with a classic parade in Red Square for the 24th Congress of the Central Committee of the Communist Party, with banners touting the same slogans from the previous forty years about production targets being met ahead of schedule. Next comes the GUM department store and window displays with tuxedos, shiny patent leather shoes and beaded handbags, making us wonder who in early 1970s Moscow was buying such luxury goods. Commercialized religion makes its first appearance with a lively trade in Christmas decorations, one of many reminders that despite an official policy of atheism, certain traditions were allowed to persist. (Vladimir Putin, of course, has done an even better job in harnessing religion to his oligarchic dictatorship.) From the capital the footage moves east, where consumer goods are far more difficult to obtain. In Suzdal, an old woman washes clothes in an ice hole; shots of Vladimir show a town seemingly unchanged from pre-Revolutionary days; further south, residents come out for a winter carnival whose roots must date long before Leninism arrived. As the cameramen spread east, local customs become stronger: Bactrian camel races near the Mongolian border, reindeer sleds in the Sakha Republic. It’s here in Siberia where the footage most forcefully critiques Soviet policy, as a group of young Caucasian Russians (in classic 1970s fashion) play guitar and sing Russian songs, the local Yakut population looking on from the sidelines, discontented observers of this not-so-subtle form of colonialism. The greatest takeaway from “Imperium” is just how stubbornly resistant centuries-old traditions were to the Soviet push towards uniformity. People still attended mosques in Bukhara and churches in Etchmiadzin, they held on to ways of life that had not been collectivized by Stalinist dictates. Today, however, rampant capitalism and the internet have changed Russia’s social landscape far more than anything Lenin or Brezhnev could have imagined, turning stubbornly multicultural populations that boldly resisted homogeneity into consumers looking West for their acquisitions. It’s interesting to imagine what might have happened had Italian TV screened the majority of these films upon release. A sense of what life was really like in the Soviet Union was hard to come by then — in the U.S., a 1977 National Geographic publication “Journey Across Russia: The Soviet Union Today” was the first populist corrective to the sense of a uniform society of collectivized proletariat. Italy, with its strong communist party, had a different problem, too often refusing to acknowledge Politburo abuses. An interesting companion piece to “Imperium” would be Federico Ferrone and Michele Manzolini’s 2013 documentary “The Train to Moscow: A Journey to Utopia,” also consisting of found footage but earlier, when a party supporter from Emilia Romagna discovered that life in the USSR wasn’t all solidarity and freedom. At the time, his Italian colleagues censored his revelations. All empires peddle utopias, but why do so many people believe them? ‘Imperium’ Review: Sergei Loznitsa Brings Together Nearly Three Hours of Italian Footage From the Early 1970s Covering the Vastness of the USSR Reviewed at Venice Film Festival (Venice Open - Documentary), Sept. 5, 2026.
