title: Festival Leaders Confront Growing Political Pressure at Lumiere Summit: ‘We Don’t Judge Artists by Their Passport’
full_text: Sep 7, 2026 5:09am PT Festival Leaders Confront Growing Political Pressure at Lumiere Summit: ‘We Don’t Judge Artists by Their Passport’ By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Festival Leaders Confront Growing Political Pressure at Lumiere Summit: ‘We Don’t Judge Artists by Their Passport’ 2 hours ago Screen Industries Adopt Five Thematic Declarations at Lumiere Summit, Setting Terms on AI, Piracy, Gender, Education and the Environment 5 hours ago France and Korea Launch $1.16 Billion Screen Industry Financing Partnership at Lumiere Summit 5 hours ago See All Naman Ramachandran Political pressure on film and television festivals emerged as a defining theme of a panel discussion Monday at the Lumière Summit in Saint-Paul-de-Vence, France, with Séries Mania general director Laurence Herszberg issuing the session’s most direct call for protection of programming autonomy. “We don’t judge artists by their passport, we judge them by their works,” Herszberg said. Related Stories Meet Topic, the Indie Studio Dominating the Festival Circuit With ‘The Debut,’ ‘Club Kid,’ ‘Wicker’ ‘The Idiot(s)’ Review: Dostoevsky Is an Endearing Drunken Fool in This Rambunctious, Tonally Off-Kilter Two-Hander The panel, titled “Easy to Criticize, Impossible to Replace: Rethinking the Festival” and moderated by Rajendra Roy, chief curator of film at MoMA, brought together festival chiefs from Berlin, Cannes, Toronto, San Sebastián, Annecy, Mumbai, Durban, the Red Sea and South by Southwest. It covered three areas: audiences and community, how festivals relate to the media, and the mounting economic and political strains on festival leadership. Herszberg was direct on the political pressure facing her and her peers. “We feel more and more under pressure from different groups,” she said. “They might be politicians, they might be just people who disagree with the representation of some countries.” As general director of Séries Mania – a free-access festival with 1,500 seats – she said controlling who walks through the door is not possible. “We have to be protected, and we still have to go on and fight for the artists,” Herszberg said. Popular on Variety Cameron Bailey, chief executive of the Toronto Film Festival, which launches its first formal market this year, echoed the sentiment. “Filmmakers are not their nations, and shouldn’t be treated as such by anyone,” Bailey said. He recalled joining TIFF as a programmer in 1990, “at a time when festivals felt like a completely free and open space.” Bailey pointed to TIFF’s Next Wave youth program – now 15 years old – as a long-term investment in building young audiences. “‘Obsession’ became one of the biggest sales at a film festival in a long, long time,” Bailey said, noting that Next Wave participants had championed the title. On the rationale for TIFF’s new market, Bailey said: “The market is also part of that ecosystem – I mean, a terrible way to put it would be that it’s the fertilizer of the ecosystem, but really, it’s what feeds” a constant supply of ambitious films. Berlinale festival director Tricia Tuttle, whose event drew 450,000 admissions last year, and was at the eye of a political storm, put audience development at the center of her contribution. “The answer for me to all of these challenges is to really think about audiences,” Tuttle said, adding that reaching people who are not yet passionate cinemagoers matters as much as serving those who are. Cannes president Iris Knobloch pointed to the breadth of her festival’s annual gathering – 40,000 accredited participants from 140 countries, with over 4,000 journalists in attendance. “For me, that is the real shining light on films and the talent all over the world,” Knobloch said. Faisal Baltyuor, chief executive of the Red Sea Film Foundation, said his organization’s last edition sold out every screening. “We have a lot of creative talents that need that boost to make it to the international stage,” Baltyuor said, noting that 11 films the Foundation supported appeared in Venice and eight were heading to Toronto. On the festival-press relationship, Peter Debruge – now director of the South by Southwest Film & TV Festival after a 20-year tenure at Variety , the last ten as chief critic – put the case for studio films serving discovery. “The studio-level films are the sizzle that brings the attention, the press, and the audiences to the discoveries,” Debruge said. Maialen Beloki, deputy director of San Sebastián, pointed to shrinking press resources as a structural problem. “Each year, media send less and less critics to the festival,” Beloki said. She added that the race to break news online carries its own cost. “We are losing our capacity to talk about the films with some time and with some respect,” Beloki said. Shivendra Singh Dungarpur, founding director of the Film Heritage Foundation and director of the MAMI Festival in Mumbai, said his screenings of restored films regularly attract between 1,000 and 1,400 people and that all MAMI events are free of charge. “I believe that a film festival has to be for everyone,” Dungarpur said. He described the MAMI Independent outreach initiative that partnered with a major cinema chain to bring independent films to cities across India ahead of the festival proper. Mickaël Marin, from the Annecy Animation Film Festival, said that since his appointment in 2018 he has worked to open Annecy to general audiences beyond its traditional professional base, including through a permanent exhibition space that opened last June. “We have a worldwide community of animation coming here in Annecy, from the school, from the student, up to the platform,” Marin said. Magdalene Reddy, director of the Durban FilmMart Institute, said the core challenge in Africa is not finding audiences but reaching them in the absence of sufficient cinema infrastructure. “For us, engaging with audiences is really going into the community,” Reddy said. When moderator Roy closed the session by asking whether festivals could survive without the American industry – demanding a yes or no – Reddy was the only panelist to answer no, while noting that her focus remains squarely on African content. title: ‘Plaza Catedral’ Director Abner Benaim, Chile’s Daniela Vega and Alfredo Castro Board Fiction Series ‘School of the Americas’ (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Sep 7, 2026 4:57am PT ‘Plaza Catedral’ Director Abner Benaim, Chile’s Daniela Vega and Alfredo Castro Board Fiction Series ‘School of the Americas’ (EXCLUSIVE) The project has been selected for the Co-Production and Financing Forum at Madrid-based confab Iberseries & Platino Industria which takes place Sept. 29-Oct. 2 By Anna Marie de la Fuente Plus Icon Anna Marie de la Fuente @adelafuente1 Latest ‘Plaza Catedral’ Director Abner Benaim, Chile’s Daniela Vega and Alfredo Castro Board Fiction Series ‘School of the Americas’ (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago ‘Strawberry and Chocolate’ Star Jorge Perugorría and Brazil’s Thiago Lacerda Lead Havana-Set ‘Hotel Nacional’ (EXCLUSIVE) 7 hours ago Mexico’s Venice Queer Lion Contender ‘Tijuana, Todavía’ Trains a Spotlight on the Plight of Gay Refugees Fleeing Persecution 2 days ago See All 'School of the Americas' Courtesy of La Panda and Seedling Media Panama’s Abner Benaim has boarded as a co-director of the fiction series “School of the Americas” (“Escuela de las Américas”), which will star two of Chile’s most internationally renowned thespians: Daniela Vega , who headed the Oscar-winning “A Fantastic Woman,) and Alfredo Castro , a Pablo Larrain regular who’s also starred in a slew of Latin American projects. The project has been selected for the Co-Production and Financing Forum at Madrid-based confab Iberseries & Platino Industria which takes place Sept. 29-Oct. 2. Related Stories Meet Topic, the Indie Studio Dominating the Festival Circuit With ‘The Debut,’ ‘Club Kid,’ ‘Wicker’ Jordan Firstman's 'Club Kid' Hits Telluride, and Colleen Camp Could Be Its Secret Oscar Weapon Benaim was an obvious addition to the project given its subject matter and setting. “School of the Americas” begins with an exhumation at the site of the 1983 El Jazmín massacre, which yields a graduation photograph of four commandos with their faces scratched out and a pendant stamped Fort Gulick, the U.S. military base in the Panama Canal Zone, site of the infamous U.S. Army School of the Americas. Popular on Variety Panamanian-American human rights investigator Inés Vega recognizes the massacre’s signature: counterinsurgency doctrine taught at the School. When someone tries to kill her, the cold case turns personal. Tracking four graduates across three continents, she uncovers what the School really taught – and who is still protecting its legacy. Benaim joins co-director Oscar Godoy who also has close ties to Larraín, having been first AD on Larraín’s “The Count,” “The Club,” “Neruda,” “No” and “Tony Manero.” Godoy was recently second unit director on Fabula ’s “Someone Has to Know,” which ranked among Netflix’s global top ten for non-English-language series. His feature “Ulysses” screened at a string of festivals, starting with the San Sebastián Film Fest and culminating at Chile’s Santiago Film Fest (Sanfic) where it won Best Chilean Film. Benaim, Panama’s most internationally renowned filmmaker, has represented his country three times at the Oscars, starting with his documentary “Invasion,” about the U.S. 1989 invasion of Panama, followed by “Yo No Me Llamo Rubén Blades” and “Plaza Catedral,” the latter making the Academy shortlist and earning Benaim a Premios Platino nomination for screenplay. His debut feature “Chance” remains the highest-grossing Panamanian film ever released. Its producers Seedling Media Productions (Panama) and La Panda Productions (U.S./Spain) are targeting 2028 for principal photography to begin, provided all the financing is in place. “The School of the Americas was a real school, located in the Panama Canal Zone; for half a century, it taught officers from across Latin America. We are not making a series about monsters — monsters are an alibi. We are making one about a curriculum: the fact that this was written down, graded and taught, and the men who graduated went home and became somebody’s father. Violence isn’t born. It’s taught,” said La Panda’s Guillermo Escalona, co-creator and executive producer alongside Brittany DeVries of Seedling Media. Escalona, a Spanish-American screenwriter-producer based in Los Angeles, co-founder of La Panda Productions, is the co-creator and co-writer, along with Rhayuela’s Federico Durán, of the late Colombian filmmaker Jaime Osorio Márquez ’s posthumous feature “The Awakening.” The supernatural action thriller was completed by Durán and José Luis Rugeles (“Alias Maria” “Rebellion”) after the director’s death following which it world-premiered at the Guadalajara International Film Festival in April, with Latido Films handling sales. Based in Panama, Seedling Media Productions, founded in 2013 by DeVries, has a varied list of credits that include fiction and documentary features. Among them are crime thriller “Chacalería,” “I Really Love My Husband,” shot in Panama and premiered at SXSW in 2025 and documentaries “Dear Panamá,” “A World Without Orphans” and “Lost Kites,” winner of the Best Documentary Feature at the London Independent Film Awards. Currently, Seedling is producing “Against No One” (“Denuncia Contra Nadie”), a co-production with Guatemala supported by the Ibermedia Co-Production Fund. title: Laura Poitras Shares the Desperate Vision Behind Her ICE Documentary ‘They’re Here’: “What’s Happening in the United States Is a Nightmare”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Patrick Brzeski Plus Icon Patrick Brzeski Asia Bureau Chief View All September 7, 2026 4:53am 'They're Here' Courtesy of Jack Califano Oscar-winning filmmaker Laura Poitras spoke bluntly at the Venice Film Festival Monday about the motivations behind her latest project, They’re Here , a 25-minute documentary that viscerally chronicles the Minneapolis resistance movement to ICE’s paramilitary occupation last year. “We believed in a sense of urgency in documenting this,” Poitras said of the film origins. “What we’re seeing in the United States is a nightmare, and we feel what’s happening in the mainstream media is that this kind of violence is being normalized. We believe very strongly in the power of cinema to denormalize this violence and to show what’s happening, so that you can feel the sense of terror.” They’re Here is Poitras’s first project since her Nan Goldin documentary All the Beauty and the Bloodshed , which won the festival’s Golden Lion in 2022 and later earned an Oscar nomination. Poitras previously won the best documentary Oscar in 2015 for Citizenfour , her landmark account of Edward Snowden and his NSA surveillance disclosures. Related Stories Movies 'Woman Unknown' Review: A Sharp, Haunting Portrait of Denmark's Post-War Reckoning Movies 'Mr. Nelson, Did You Kill People?' Review: A Vietnam Vet Reckons With PTSD in a Heavy-Handed Trauma Drama Poitras co-directed They’re Here with Minneapolis-based journalist and documentarian Rachel Lauren Mueller. Told in the style of dystopian sci-fi cinema, the film starts in a picturesque wintry American Midwest landscape — but this is Trump’s America in 2025, where masked men are soon shown abducting children, as residents hide in the trunks of cars to safely get to work. Elsewhere, everyday American vacationers mill about at Minneapolis’ airport, gazing out the windows at shackled prisoners being dragged onboard planes nearby. They’re Here draws on dashcam footage, crowdsourced data visualizations and ground-level footage to reconstruct the resistance network and the cat-and-mouse surveillance tactics used by residents and ICE’s masked agents. “We were using the genres or language of dystopian cinema or horror to take us closer to reality, not to take us further away, and not to make fiction from reality,” Poitras explained in Venice. “This actually is the reality — the reality is a nightmare. The entire country is under attack, and immigrants are living in fear throughout the United States right now.” “Over the two Trump terms, we’ve seen that things have gotten more extreme, but people become used to certain things,” added Mueller. “So I think the real role of this film is to shake that up a bit — to change things from a space of intellectualization about these numbers and these images that we see, and to have it become more visceral again.” Poitras explained that the doc, like the resistance movement at its heart, emerged from a sense of solidarity with the immigrants who had made Minneapolis their home. “It came from a real sense of, ‘These are our neighbors, and we don’t want them stolen from us. We want these people to stay safe,'” she said. She also sees causes for both hope and despair in the Trump administration’s response to Minneapolis’ resistance, which she described as a “great success.” “At the end of the film, we say how these tens and hundreds of thousands of residents responded, and that ICE removed 80 percent of its agents. So there was a real response to this kind of resistance, which I think we can all take hope from,” she explained. “At the same time, ICE has a budget of $70 billion, which is just an astronomical amount of money. Additionally, in the last two months, 90,000 people were abducted. So it’s this is a record high that has happened in June and July. So ICE is absolutely still active. Their tactics just look very different now.” They’re Here is screening in Venice Open – Out of Competition, the festival’s nonfiction and special-presentation strand, and will have its world premiere in the Sala Grande on Monday afternoon. The film was produced by Mueller, Poitras and longtime Poitras collaborator Yoni Golijov, with ARTE France serving as co-producer. Submarine Entertainment Sales is handling U.S. sales. THR

title: ‘Sumo: Spirit Weighs Nothing’ Review: A Handsome Ode to an Oft-Disrespected Sport
full_text: Sep 7, 2026 4:50am PT ‘Sumo: Spirit Weighs Nothing’ Review: A Handsome Ode to an Oft-Disrespected Sport Erik Shirai's ESPN-produced Venice premiere follows a year in the lives of several men at ascending and descending stages of their relatively short sumo careers. By Guy Lodge Plus Icon Guy Lodge Film Critic @guylodge Latest ‘Sumo: Spirit Weighs Nothing’ Review: A Handsome Ode to an Oft-Disrespected Sport 3 hours ago ‘Agata the Writer’ Review: Mia Wasikowska Plays an Author Adrift and Short of Ideas, in a Sly, Witty Film With Plenty 20 hours ago ‘Chronovisor’ Review: An Eerie, Fiendishly Clever Mystery for Lovers of Libraries and the Storied Smell of Old Books 2 days ago See All ESPN Films The title of “ Sumo: Spirit Weighs Nothing ” is the closest that Erik Shirai ‘s documentary comes to a joke at the expense of its subject: sumo wrestling, the Japanese sport largely known in the western world for the ample size and minimal clothing of its practitioners, and not an awful lot beyond that. In all other respects, however, this stately, artfully produced film aims to act as a corrective to such cheap, culturally insensitive perceptions. Examining as it does the motivations and ambitions of a number of sumo wrestlers, from grand masters to rising stars, through a solemnly respectful lens, the doc finds humanity and even beauty in what can all too easily be comically framed on screen. Related Stories Telluride’s Julie Huntsinger on Her 20 Years Leading the Festival, Chasing ‘Digger’ and ‘Dune 3’ and a ‘True TBA’ Film Hidden Until Patrons Walk Into the Theater Telluride Festival Lineup: 'The Debut,' 'Elsinore' and 'Tender Loving Care' Set for Premieres, Tributes for John Malkovich, Sandra Hüller and Andrew Haigh Indeed, the approach of Japanese-American docmaker Shirai (who previously probed a very different Japanese institution in his popular 2015 doc “The Birth of Saké”) is so respectful as to feel a touch sanitized: smoothed-out and simplified for the benefit of Western viewers, to whose perspective the film is mostly tailored. More unsavory aspects of the sport — including controversies over hazing and match-fixing, not to mention its ongoing exclusion of women from competition and ceremonies — are swept aside, while the compelling fact of its declining popularity in Japan is only passingly addressed. Only before the closing credits roll is it revealed how few yokozuna (the name given to men achieving the highest rank in sumo) this century have been homegrown, as Mongolia and the U.S. step into the breach. Popular on Variety Shedding more light on such matters would provide a richer context for the film’s reverent celebration of sumo tradition, but many viewers will still find it an illuminating and exquisitely mounted study, ennobling the sport with the sheer, studied splendor of its imagery, captured alternately in atmospherically high-contrast monochrome and tea-stained sepia tones. Produced by ESPN Films, it will doubtless find a dedicated broadcast and streaming viewership following its premiere as the opening film of Venice’s audience-oriented Spotlight competition. Early on, the camera observes a group of rookie wrestlers, training at the Tokyo stable of 62-year-old Master Sakaigawa, as they collectively recite a pledge to the sport: “We shall uphold our responsibility and duty to to sumo; we shall uphold a strong heart, kindness and courage.” This is followed by a droll shot of trainees all putting their freshly laundered thongs out to dry: For all its earnestness, the film is not without offhand humor. In the house of Sakaigawa, we meet Hiradoumi, a 24-year-old upstart tipped for big things in the ring (or dohyō , to use its proper term), and a great hope for continued Japanese representation in the sport’s top tier. In the same stable, and younger still, is teenager Yonezawaryu, still learning the ropes, and battling doubts over his long-term commitment to sumo after witnessing firsthand the extreme, potentially fatal, physical toll it takes on the body. At the opposite end of the career scale is Mongolian-born Terunofuji, who at the time of filming was the only practicing yokozuna in sumo, a 10-time title winner considering retirement after 14 years in the sport, five of them at the very top. He is spoken of as a veteran, positively godly in status, though he’s only 33 years old. Age, however, doesn’t mean quite what it does to civilians in a realm where so much transformational strain is placed on the body, and Terunofuji’s is beginning to fail him. “By doing sumo, I’m cutting my lifespan by 10 to 20 years,” he frankly admits, before likening the travails of the professional wrestler to those of a soldier going to war. He’s now married with a son — it’s hard not to wonder if, at the end of his reign, he thinks it was all worth it. It’s one of a few questions that this handsome, sober documentary is too polite to ask. But it does convey the grand, challenging physicality of sumo, which to many of its students qualifies as an answer in itself. There’s also a thoughtful focus here on the pain and labor that goes into building and maintaining these extraordinary bodies — shot, by Shirai and fellow DP Hiroshi Hara, in awed chiaroscuro portraits that line up with the men’s view of themselves as warriors of a kind, leaving far behind many racist, cartoonish depictions of yore. ‘Sumo: Spirit Weighs Nothing’ Review: A Handsome Ode to an Oft-Disrespected Sport Reviewed at Soho Screening Rooms, London, Aug. 13, 2026. title: Belgian Royalty Series ‘King of Hearts’ Secures Key VRT Backing (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Sep 7, 2026 4:46am PT Belgian Royalty Series ‘King of Hearts’ Secures Key VRT Backing (EXCLUSIVE) By Anna Marie de la Fuente Plus Icon Anna Marie de la Fuente @adelafuente1 Latest ‘Plaza Catedral’ Director Abner Benaim, Chile’s Daniela Vega and Alfredo Castro Board Fiction Series ‘School of the Americas’ (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago Belgian Royalty Series ‘King of Hearts’ Secures Key VRT Backing (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago ‘Strawberry and Chocolate’ Star Jorge Perugorría and Brazil’s Thiago Lacerda Lead Havana-Set ‘Hotel Nacional’ (EXCLUSIVE) 7 hours ago See All 'King of Hearts' Courtesy of De Wereldvrede Enterprising Flemish broadcaster VRT has boarded the historical coming-of-age drama series ‘King of Hearts’ from Giles Coulier, whose company, De Wereldvrede , is behind such hits as 2019 series “War of the Worlds” and Prix Europa winner, “Albatros.” As continental royalty series hit ratins and sales – think “Maxima” – “King of Hearts,” currently in development, has been selected to participate in the inaugural Euro-Atlantic Co-Pro Pitch program to be held at the Iberseries & Platino Industria confab in Madrid. Related Stories At Telluride Film Festival, Bill Gates Compares Lack of Control Over AI to HAL in '2001': 'You Could Say "Please Shut Down," and It Would Say, "OK, I Took That Under Advisement, But..."' Telluride’s Julie Huntsinger on Her 20 Years Leading the Festival, Chasing ‘Digger’ and ‘Dune 3’ and a ‘True TBA’ Film Hidden Until Patrons Walk Into the Theater Based on real events, the drama centers on Baudouin, introverted and insecure, who is made King before he is ready for the task. As Belgium descends into crisis and his family fractures around him, he is forced to confront the man and leader he wants to become. Under mounting pressure, he learns to make difficult choices, challenge his father’s influence and forge his own beliefs. But with power comes a darker temptation: to control others as he himself was once controlled. Popular on Variety Later in life, he tries to protect his nephew Filip from the same painful path he went through. But he slowly realizes how hard it is to become a better man than the father who raised him. “We are thrilled we can once again work on a fiction series that sheds light on an important chapter in our recent history. As a public broadcaster, we believe it is essential to tell these stories, but always through emotionally compelling, surprising and strong storytelling,” said Elly Vervloet, VRT international drama expert. “’King of Hearts is the coming-of-age story of King Baudouin, who, as a young and unprepared prince, had to ascend the throne at a politically very delicate moment for our country and the whole world. We see him struggle to find his own voice, torn between power and responsibility, manipulated by people around him with their own agendas. We are thrilled that the producers and creators of De Wereldvrede approached us with this story, so that we can develop it further together into an ambitious and emotionally resonant series. We hope to bring some strong international partners on board to bring this fascinating story to audiences far beyond Belgium.” For producer Gilles De Schryver, who co-founded De Wereldvrede with Coulier in 2013, “King of Hearts” is by nature an international story. “It moves between Brussels, Leopoldville, Rome and Madrid, intertwining Belgium’s monarchy with Congolese independence, Cold War geopolitics and Catholic influence. It is designed as a high-value prestige drama with global story reach and appeal only an international co-production can deliver.” The project has secured script funding from the Flanders Audiovisual Fund (VAF), with a further VAF application pending. According to the partners, De Wereldvrede’s “mission is to produce high-quality fiction for an international market, with a strong emphasis on the creator’s vision and a bottom-up production approach.” The company broke through with the TV series “The Natives” (CANVAS), followed by Coulier’s feature film “Cargo,” which screened at numerous international festivals. Their short films have also earned recognition, including “Stephanie,” an official Cannes selection and winner of the Ensor for Best Short Film, and the series “Lockdown,” which won an award at Canneseries. “Roomies” (2022) received international acclaim. In 2024, the features “Holy Rosita” and “Julie Keeps Quiet” premiered internationally, earning numerous festival selections and awards. “Julie Keeps Quiet” premiered at Cannes Critics’ Week and was selected as Belgium’s official Oscar entry. Both films won five Ensor Awards. In October 2025, the second season of “Roomies,” by Kato De Boeck and Flo Van Deuren, premiered at Film Fest Gent to five-star reviews. Nathalie Teirlinck’s second feature, “Jonah Was Here,” is currently in post-production, while Pieter Van Hees’ latest film, “Alors on Danse,” is in advanced development and scheduled to shoot in summer 2027. De Wereldvrede is also developing several other projects, including the feature films “Harvest,” “The Right to Say Goodbye” and “Dirty Kids,” as well as the fiction series “Recidive” and “Beats of Love.” The 6 th Iberseries & Platino Industria runs September 29 to October 2, 2026. title: Tom Rothman on Sony’s ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Blockbuster Success, Being Outbid for ‘Obsession’ and More
full_text: Sep 7, 2026 4:13am PT Tom Rothman on Sony’s ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Blockbuster Success, Being Outbid for ‘Obsession’ and More By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest Tom Rothman on Sony’s ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Blockbuster Success, Being Outbid for ‘Obsession’ and More 4 hours ago Tetris Company Distances Itself From Trump White House’s ‘Build the Wall’ Game, Says ‘We Take Copyright Very Seriously’ 3 days ago Digital Creator Skyelar Chase Signs With Innovative Artists Entertainment 3 days ago See All Getty Images Sony’s Tom Rothman took a bit of a victory lap with the studio’s boffo success of “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” which has become the highest-grossing film of 2026 to date. Rothman, chairman and CEO of Sony Pictures Entertainment ‘s Motion Picture Group, spoke Monday at the Lumière Summit in Saint-Paul-de-Vence, an international film and entertainment conference hosted by the French government. He was interviewed at the event by Variety co-editor-in-chief Cynthia Littleton. Related Stories Telluride Festival Lineup: 'The Debut,' 'Elsinore' and 'Tender Loving Care' Set for Premieres, Tributes for John Malkovich, Sandra Hüller and Andrew Haigh Nathan Fielder Drops Weird Trailer for Secret Elizabeth Holmes Doc ‘You Can See Everything’ Since its July 31 release, “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” has spun up a whopping $2.4 billion at the global box office, including $923 million domestically. About the success of the film, Rothman joked, “First of all, I can’t be wrong all the time. It’s against the law of averages.” Popular on Variety More seriously, he said, “For a result like that to happen, everything has to work perfectly.” Rothman praised the “incredibly talented” team that worked on the films, including star Tom Holland, who “has been our partner in this for over a decade now,” as well as the support of Disney and Marvel. Why have audiences turned out in droves to see it? Rothman said “Brand New Day” is “not so much a superhero film, but ‘super-person’ film. The reason that movie has resonated all around the world is because it’s about a lonely guy… It’s like yeah, it’s about friendship. It’s very human. It’s very emotional.” He said, “It’s got plenty of whiz-bang, but that’s not what the secret is. The secret is it’s a relatable story that almost everybody has related to.” Referring to the opening session at the Lumière Summit, at which French President Emmanuel Macron and South Korean President Lee Jae Myung unveiled a $1.16 billion entertainment industry financing partnership , Rothman said, “We had three presidents today: The president of France, the president of Korea. And you have Mr. Clooney , the president of Hollywood” — gesturing to George Clooney, who was sitting in the front row. Alluding to Mark Twain’s famous quote, Rothman said this summer in particular has demonstrated that the death of the theatrical business has been greatly exaggerated. This summer, “movies were cool,” Rothman said. “They became cultural again… because they were culturally significant.” In particular, Rothman called out “Obsession,” the low-budget horror film reportedly made for $700,000 that has banked nearly $510 million at the global box office. He said the success of “Obsession” shows that “it’s a misnomer that young people won’t go to movies.” Sony Pictures was outbid for Curry Barker’s “Obsession” by “a couple million dollars” by Universal’s Focus Features, which reportedly paid $14 million for the rights . When Sony was outbid, Rothman joshed, “I was outraged.” But, he added, “I would like to have that moment back. I congratulate the worthy opposition.” Speaking about Sony’s global film business, Rothman said that Netflix “was brave enough at the time” to finance animated musical movie “K-Pop Demon Hunters,” which has become the streamer’s most-viewed film ever. “That is a deeply Korean, culturally relevant film,” he said. The key having a globally resonant film or TV show, Rothman said, is to have it be specific to a time and place. “Specificity leads to universality,” he said. “I have seen it many times in my career.” Sony, for example, now has a big Japanese anime business, “and it does great.” “Stories are the things that… become our cultural heritage,” said Rothman. Rothman joined Sony Pictures in 2013 as chairman of TriStar Pictures before being promoted to chairman of Sony Pictures Motion Picture Group in February 2015 and then chairman/CEO in 2021. title: Ellen Burstyn on Being “Recognized” by Marilyn Monroe, Changing Roles for Women With ‘Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore’
full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All September 7, 2026 3:25am Ellen Burstyn Tiziana FABI / AFP via Getty Images Ellen Burstyn never met Marilyn Monroe. Not properly, anyway. By the time she walked through the doors of the Actors Studio in New York, Monroe was already dead. But the two women did see each other once, across a nightclub table, and Burstyn has been carrying the moment around for the better part of six decades. “I was enchanted just looking at her. She was such a magical creature,” Burstyn recalled, speaking to reporters at the Venice Film Festival, where she is presenting two films this year and will receive an honorary Golden Lion for lifetime achievement at a ceremony this evening. “And then she looked at me and nodded at me. I was very early in my career, and I thought: I’ve just been recognized by Marilyn Monroe. I carried that in my heart.” Related Stories Movies Gary Oldman Says a James Bond Has Been Picked -- and He's Hoping It's Jack Lowden TV Catherine Zeta-Jones' Real Swansea Accent Is Loud and Proud in Trailer for AMC+'s 'Kill Jackie' Burstyn plays a version of Monroe, an imagined projection as if the legendary actress had lived into her 90s, in Flesh Impact , a new short film from director Maggie Gyllenhaal ( The Bride! ). Dakota Johnson plays the younger Monroe in flashbacks. She also appears in Kornél Mundruczó’s drama Place to Be , which screens out of competition in Venice, as an elderly woman who strikes up an unlikely friendship with a middle-aged divorced man (played by Taika Waititi). “He’s the most talented, funny, nice, charming, adorable human being I’ve ever worked with,” said Burstyn. “The movie is about our relationship, and of course he’s a young man compared to me, and I’m much older, so it’s not a sexual relationship, but it is a love relationship [and] that’s what I think people are going to respond to.” Asked how the role of women in Hollywood has changed since she started out, the actress didn’t hesitate: “Oh my goodness. Enormously.” “When I first started working, which was 150 years ago,” the 93-year-old added, drawing a laugh, “there were no women on the set. There were no women in the crew. Nobody. It was all men. If a woman was on the set, then she was an actress.” The change, she said, came slowly and incrementally, one job at a time: first a script supervisor, then a camera assistant, then more. “Slowly that changed, until finally it’s gotten to the point where women are handling heavy equipment without even thinking about it, and they’re integrated into the crew.” The roles themselves took longer, and Burstyn had a hand in forcing that particular door open. The origin story of Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore , the 1974 road movie that won her the Academy Award for best actress, begins on the set of The Exorcist . John Calley, then running Warner Bros., called her agent and said the studio wanted to make another film with her. The scripts started arriving. “Every one of them was this old-fashioned idea of what women represent,” she said. “I didn’t recognize any of the characters as anything like the women I knew, or myself. Their husbands would go out and save the world, and when they came home, the women would hand them a cup of tea. It was that kind of supportive role.” So she made a counteroffer. “I said, ‘Well, I’d like to make a film about women as I know women to be.'” For a director, she picked “an unknown director” with a single feature to his name: Martin Scorsese . His working method, she said, shaped the film as much as the screenplay did. At the end of each shooting day, the company would rehearse the following day’s scene — and improvise through it. “That script grew into a film that I think is credited with helping to change the consciousness of women worldwide.” The Exorcist , by contrast, she described as both transformative and brutal. William Friedkin was “an extremely talented director,” she said, “but he was also one of those directors who would do anything to get a shot” — including, in her case, a back injury she says she should never have sustained. “It was a life-changing experience, but it was painful physically.” Asked about the through-line in her memoir — the way her discovery of herself as an actress ran parallel to her discovery of herself as a woman — Burstyn credited her decades studying with Lee Strasberg at the Actors’ Studio. “When you study with a master, it changes your life,” she said. “It changes who you are to yourself, because it brings you into areas not only of your art but of your own being and your own understanding. And it changes what you do forever.” The work never stopped, either. Even after winning the Oscar [for Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore ], and after Strasberg had put her in front of a classroom to teach, she was still turning up as a student. “I was still working for him,” she said, “bringing in scenes, bringing in difficult things.” The octogenarian mainly avoided politics during the talk, with only a side mention that “my country right now is providing a lot of material to be explored artistically and politically.” Asked if she had any advice for younger actresses coming up, Burstyn recounted her own encounter, early in her career, with a screen legend of her youth. “I met Bette Davis. She said, ‘the only thing that’s important is your work. Anybody tries to get in the way of you and your work. They’re your enemy’,” Burstyn recalled. “So that was my advice from the older generation.” THR

title: BBC News Presenter Maryam Moshiri Reveals She Has Incurable Blood Cancer
full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake Piers Morgan Launches ‘Football Uncensored’ On YouTube After World Cup Series Scored 60M Views BBC Rejects Complaints It Aired “Too Much” Coverage Of Harry & Meghan’s UK Return BBC News Presenter Maryam Moshiri Reveals She Has Incurable Blood Cancer View All September 7, 2026 2:23am BBC News channel presenter Maryam Moshiri BBC News Maryam Moshiri , one of the BBC’s most seasoned news presenters, has revealed that she has been diagnosed with blood cancer. In interviews with BBC News and The Times of London , Moshiri said that she is living with polycythaemia vera, a rare but treatable blood cancer. Moshiri, 49, was diagnosed in November 2024 after her doctor was “fastidious” about blood tests. Moshiri said she “mostly” had no symptoms, though the condition can cause headaches, confusion, dizziness, and blurred vision. Polycythaemia vera is manageable with treatment. Moshiri has received “debilitating” rounds of venesection, which involves bloodletting. She has also received immunotherapy. Related Stories News Deborah Turness Resurfaces With Studio At Independent Talent Group News BBC To Test Streaming News Channel Live On YouTube Outside Of UK The cancer can thicken the blood, increasing the risk of developing blood clots that can lead to strokes, heart attacks, or deep vein thrombosis. Watch on Deadline “It’s been two years since my diagnosis and I’ve felt that I’ve started to understand the disease a lot better and the way it affects my life. I’ve got a handle on it to a degree now, so I felt it was really important to raise awareness,” Moshiri told BBC News. On the venesection treatment, she said: “In about a space of five months, I had venesection seven or eight times. So you can imagine my iron levels hit the floor and I felt even more exhausted. “After a while, I started feeling extremely unwell and tired. I started losing my hair, I got itchy all over my body, but the main symptom was fatigue.” She continued: “It’s the kind of fatigue that is not like I’m just tired and I didn’t get a good night’s sleep, you feel like someone has removed your battery completely, and however much sleep you get makes no difference.” Moshiri has continued to work over the past two years, traveling overseas to anchor BBC News, including spending time in Qatar at the start of the U.S.-Israel war with Iran. “Even though I feel the best I have in two years, I don’t know how I’m going to be in six months, one year, two years,” she said. “People with PV have a higher chance of stroke, heart attack or DVT, so it’s something I always have to be aware of and make sure I mitigate.” Netflix Confirms Third ‘Inbetweeners’ Movie; First Look At Cast ‘Possible Love’ Rave Reaction; ‘Woman Unknown’ Snafu; Reviews; Photos Nights 1-2 Full Winners List; Rob Reiner Posthumous Win; Red Carpet Pix Surprise Movie ‘You Can See Everything’ Reviewed; More Pics In Focus Read More About: 1 Comments

title: Gaza Cinema Academy Launches At Venice Film Festival To Help Gazans Tell Their Own Stories
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Gaza Cinema Academy Launches At Venice Film Festival To Help Gazans Tell Their Own Stories ‘A Good Little Soldier’ Trailer: Alba Rohrwacher & Vincent Lindon Co-Star In Stéphane Brizé’s Venice Contender Exploring Toxic Corporate Culture Netflix Officially Confirms ‘The Inbetweeners’ Reunion Movie As Production Kicks Off With First Look At Original Cast In Reprised Roles View All September 7, 2026 2:10am Ezzaldeen Shalh (c) with students on Gaza Filmmaking Diploma course Gaza Cinema Academy The official launch of the Gaza Cinema Academy was announced at the Venice Film Festival on Monday, as the humanitarian crisis in the Palestinian territory continues to dominate global news. The initiative – co-founded by Palestinian filmmakers Ezzaldeen Shalh and Mai Masri – aims to establish a sustainable space for film education, training and production in the Gaza Strip. Gaza-based director and film academic Shalh is known for works such as The Dry Spring , The Other World and Love and Bread as well as for spearheading the Gaza International Women’s Film Festival. Related Stories News 'A Good Little Soldier' Trailer: Alba Rohrwacher & Vincent Lindon Co-Star In Stéphane Brizé's Venice Contender Exploring Toxic Corporate Culture News May El-Toukhy Stops Venice Competition Screening Of 'Woman Unknown' Over Subtitle Snafu; Film Goes On To Garner 7 1/2-Minute Ovation “In Gaza, cinema is not merely an art form; it is a means of preserving memory, reclaiming our right to shape our own image, and giving a new generation the tools to tell its own story,” he said. Watch on Deadline The launch was accompanied by a short film showing Shalh in the classroom with aspiring female filmmakers talking about their desire to bring their stories to the big screen. Palestinian film and TV heavyweights Annemarie Jacir , Hiam Abbass and Saleh Bakri have gotten behind the initiative, with Egyptian comedian and filmmaker Ramy Youssef, Tunisian The Voice of Hind Rajab director Kaouther Ben Hania , who is in Venice this year as a member of the jury; Italian producer Graziella Bildesheim, and Alaa Karkouti, cofounder of Cairo-based film promotion and talent company Mad Solutions, also lending their support. The official launch of the academy is the next step in a process that began in 2024 with the development of the Gaza Filmmaking Diploma, a nine-month theoretical and practical filmmaking training which welcomed its first intake of 25 young Palestinian women in March 2026. The academy is also working to develop a filmmaking degree accredited by Al-Quds Open University, the main higher education institute for Palestinians, with the aim of establishing a sustainable academic pathway for film education in the Gaza Strip. Palestinian cinema pioneer Masri is best known for her 2015 feature 3000 Nights , which premiered in Toronto and the played numerous festivals worldwide. “Supporting a new generation of filmmakers in Gaza means giving them a space to express their reality, memory and dreams. We believe that creativity and cinema can empower, preserve human memory, and build bridges that transcend borders,” she said. Shalh invited film and cultural institutions, festivals, film funds, production companies, filmmakers and related organizations around the world to build partnerships with the Academy, to exchanging expertise, provide resources and professional opportunities. “We want the Academy to open a window for young people and women in Gaza to learn, create and make their own films, and for their voices and images to reach the world. We invite our partners in institutions, universities and the international film community to be part of building this space,” he said.
